idiom_name: AsyncStream<Order> (structured concurrency) or Combine PassthroughSubject<Order, Never>
implementation_notes: AsyncStream<Element> is a typed channel in the standard library: one AsyncStream<Order> per message type with a Continuation for the producer and a for await loop for the consumer, and the element type is the contract, so no downcasting happens on the receiving side. The bufferingPolicy chosen at construction (unbounded, bufferingNewest(n), bufferingOldest(n)) is the per-type policy - the default unbounded buffer is the one to think about explicitly. Combine's PassthroughSubject<Output, Failure> is the reactive sibling with the same typed-channel idea plus a Failure type in the signature; when several consumers must see every message, a shared/broadcast stream or a subject replaces the single AsyncSequence, which hands each element to one consumer only.
code_sketch:
var cont: AsyncStream<Order>.Continuation!
let orders = AsyncStream<Order>(bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(1000)) { cont = $0 }

Task { for await order in orders { await handle(order) } }   // type is the contract
cont.yield(order)                                            // producer side
cont.finish()                                                // ends the consumer loop
pitfalls: The continuation must be finished (cont.finish()); otherwise a for await loop never terminates and the consuming task leaks.
The default buffering policy is unbounded (Int.max), so a fast producer grows memory unless .bufferingNewest/.bufferingOldest bounds the per-type buffer.
An AsyncStream is a single sequence: two consumers compete for elements rather than both receiving them, so fan-out needs a different type (shared stream, subject or one stream per subscriber).
